newsitem.title: USA: Saab seeks input from Saturn ad agency for new sedan.
newsitem.headline: Saab seeks input from Saturn ad agency for new sedan.

text.p: Saab, which will enter the premium performance sedan market for the first time next year, is seeking marketing input from the same ad agency that has given Saturn Corp. its popular, folksy image.

Joel Mamby, president of Saab Cars USA Inc., said Monday that Hal Riney and Partners, the San Francisco agency that does Saturn ads, has been asked to provide ideas for a launch campaign for the new 9-5 sedan, which is scheduled to go on sale in the United States in March of 1998.

Saab also has asked for ideas from the Martin Agency, a unit of the Lowe Group, which handles the automaker's ads outside of the United States, as well as its existing agency, Angotti, Thomas, Hedge, said Mamby. Both Lowe and Angotti are subsidiaries of Interpublic Group of Companies Inc.

Saab, jointly owned by General Motors Corp. and Sweden's AB Investor, is trying to shed its image in the United States of a quirky Swedish car company and become a mainstream choice of luxury car buyers, Mamby said.

Mamby, one of several Saab executives who came from Saturn, also a GM car line, stopped short of saying the Saab acount was up for review. He said the 9-5 launch is critical for Saab because it takes the automaker into a market segment that people have not typically associated with Saab.

"We just want to have a couple of other people look at it," he said during a speech to the Automotive Press Association. "We can't be small, cult specialists or quaintly odd," he said, citing one of Saab's brand goals.

Saab, which nearly tripled its ad budget to $55 million two years ago, is currently running animated ads that use the tagline "Find your own road." Although the agencies are providing ideas for just the 9-5, Mamby said Saab only plans to have one ad theme for all of its product lines.
Unlike Canada, where Saab and Saturn dealerships are often paired, there are no marketing links planned between the two lines in the United States, he said.

Sales from the 9-5 and a future wagon version are expected to be a big part of the automaker's planned sales revitalization for the United States. The company hopes to sell 10,000 9-5's during its first calendar year in the United States, Mamby said.
Pricing has not been set, but Mamby said it will be "very competitive" with others in its class, such as the BMW 5-Series. The segment typically ranges from $32,000 to $42,000, he said.

By 2000, Saab is looking for annual U.S. sales to reach 40,000. That would be the highest since the company's peak year of 1986 in the United States when it sold 44,000 cars. For this year, Mamby expects U.S. sales of 31,800 vs. 28,253 in 1996.
The company, which lost $170 million in 1996, will continue to lose money in 1997 and into 1998, said Mamby. It is slated to reach full-year profits in 1999.
GM, which took over management control of the company, continues to want a strong representation from Investor on Saab's board, Mamby said.
